name: Saddamism
summary: Saddamism is the Ba'thist ideology of Saddam Hussein and of Iraq under his rule (1979-2003): pan-Arab nationalism centred on Iraq, rule by a single party fused with a personality cult around the leader, a state-led socialist economy built on nationalised oil that admitted a regulated private sector and was partly liberalised from 1987, and an anti-imperialist, anti-Zionist foreign policy. Secular into the 1980s, it turned to a state-promoted Islam with the Faith Campaign of 1993, and its record includes wars on Iran and Kuwait, the Anfal campaign against the Kurds and systematic repression of opponents.
scope: Saddam Hussein's political thought and the practice of the Iraqi state and Ba'th Party he led, as Malhotra (s6) and Baram (s7, s8) define it: his speeches, interviews and writings from the 1970s to 2001 (s1, s23-s40), the party's Ninth Regional Congress report of 1982, which presents his ideas as its guidelines (s19), and the regime's record from 1979 to 2003 as reported by the Library of Congress, Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International (s9-s18). Policies of the 1968-79 period are included where Saddam drove them as deputy (oil nationalisation, the 1970 constitution and land reform). It excludes the Syrian Ba'th, Aflaq's thought as such, and post-2003 Ba'thist insurgent groups.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The regime kept money wages throughout and in 1987 added bonuses of up to 30 percent of productivity gains for state workers (Library of Congress study).

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: Wage employment continued in both the state and private sectors, with minimum wages and working hours set by law (Library of Congress study).

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: Iraq armed and funded the Syrian Muslim Brothers against the Asad regime from 1982, when they were wholly dependent on Iraqi support (Baram).

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Ad Dawah, the Shia party working for an Islamic revolution, was banned in 1980, and other opposition parties could operate only in exile (Library of Congress study).

central-planning.rationale: Five-year plans and state investment budgets guided the economy after 1968, but war forced ad hoc planning and in 1987 Saddam turned toward privatisation (Library of Congress study).

civilians-legitimate-targets.rationale: The Anfal campaign struck Kurdish villages and their civilians with chemical weapons and mass killings (Human Rights Watch).

civilizational-union.rationale: Saddam's Ba'thism calls for political unity of the Arab states as one nation, and in 1995 he accepted a state uniting the Muslim world provided it began with Arab unity (Baram).

clerical-rule.rationale: The regime executed Ayatollah Baqir al-Sadr and banned Ad Dawah, and kept the clergy as salaried state officials under party rule (Baram; Library of Congress study).

collective-farming.rationale: In the 1970s the government set up collective state farms, but in the 1980s it judged them unprofitable, leased land to private firms and planned to sell the state farms, so the record runs both ways.

conscription.rationale: Men were liable to conscription until 45, the two-year service was extended without limit during the war, and draft dodgers were court-martialled and executed in public (Library of Congress study).

death-penalty.rationale: Executions of political prisoners and ordinary criminals, including mass 'prison cleansing' executions, were reported throughout 1999-2002 (Human Rights Watch).

decent-living-guarantee.rationale: The regime paid generous benefits to war widows and martyrs' families, pensions and social security, though in 1987 it cut subsidies to deal with war debt (Library of Congress study).

decide-locally.rationale: Decision-making stayed with the RCC in Baghdad, and the Kurdish Autonomous Region had its own bodies but no genuine self-rule (Library of Congress study).

democracy-best.rationale: Elections used a single list, candidates had to prove belief in the 1968 revolution's principles to an appointed commission, and by 1988 the promised popular democracy remained unfulfilled.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Women were drawn into ministries, construction, medicine and law enforcement during the war and sat in the National Assembly, though the law kept religious personal-status rules (Library of Congress study).

distribute-by-need.rationale: The Ninth Congress report sets the party against the communist aim of distribution according to need and defends private ownership within socialist limits.

dominated-front.rationale: Saddam wants Iraq to lead an anti-imperialist line internationally, aligned only with the masses against imperialism, and urges the Non-Aligned Movement against imperialism and Zionism.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Security offences went to the Revolutionary Court and to special security courts under the secret police, both outside the appeals system and generally closed (Library of Congress study).

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Iraq refused to meet the Security Council's disarmament conditions and suspended cooperation with UN inspectors in 1998 (Human Rights Watch 1999).

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Saddam's stated aim of a nonaligned Iraq that joins no great-power camp sets it against permanent alliances with them.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Under the Arabization policy non-Arabs who refused to re-register as Arabs were expelled and stripped of property, and non-Arab names for newborns were banned (Human Rights Watch 2001, 2003).

ethnic-nation.rationale: The constitution named Arabs and Kurds as Iraq's two nationalities, but from 1997 the Arabization policy pressed Kurds and Turkmen to register as Arabs or leave.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Against the Kurdish rebellion the regime sent two army corps and the security services, used mass executions and gassed Halabja and dozens of villages (Human Rights Watch).

force-without-un.rationale: Iraq invaded Iran in 1980 on Saddam's decision (Library of Congress study) and Kuwait in 1990, then refused the Security Council's disarmament terms (Human Rights Watch 1999).

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: The constitution in force barred foreign ownership of real estate, allowing only individual legal exemptions (Library of Congress study).

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: RCC Resolution 1646 of 1980 forbade foreign capital in private companies and foreign ownership of state firms was barred, though in 1987 the government moved to loosen these limits.

free-basic-services-for-all.rationale: Health care in state facilities and education were provided free to all citizens, workers in the private sector included (Library of Congress study).

free-public-college.rationale: The constitution in force guaranteed free education from primary school through university, and the free education programme was backed by a law making refusal to take part a crime (Library of Congress study).

harm-principle.rationale: The Faith Campaign banned public drinking, closed most nightclubs and banned betting, all conduct without harm to others (Baram).

head-commands-forces.rationale: The president, as RCC chairman, presided over the cabinet, supervised the ministers and appointed or dismissed the vice-president at will (Library of Congress study).

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: On Oil Nationalisation calls the foreign oil monopolies a state within the state endangering Iraqi independence and makes economic independence a main aim of the 1968 revolution.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Iraq kept a nuclear weapons programme that the Security Council required it to destroy as a condition for lifting sanctions (Human Rights Watch 1999).

independent-unions.rationale: State blue-collar workers belonged to government-sponsored unions while private-sector unions were banned; after 1987 state workers were barred from unions altogether (Library of Congress study).

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Saddam calls for a democratic Palestinian state of all its original inhabitants, with Jews returning to the countries they came from, in place of the Zionist entity.

job-guarantee.rationale: Until 1987 the labour law guaranteed every adult lifetime employment; Saddam's Decree 652 of 1987 abolished it, so the guarantee held for most but not all of the record.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Saddam calls the Arabs one nation sharing history, heritage and civilisation that must be united across present borders.

land-redistribution.rationale: The 1970 agrarian reform law cut the ceilings on holdings, expropriated the excess and distributed it, and a 1975 law broke up the estates of Kurdish tribal landlords.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: The record runs both ways: from 1994 Qur'anic amputation was decreed for theft, yet the civil and commercial law stayed largely secular and spirits stayed on sale (Baram).

leader-cult.rationale: Malhotra documents Saddam's face on offices, schools, airports, shops and every banknote, school songs in his praise and the spread of his books as means of promoting Saddamism.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Decree 118 of 1994 made organising prostitution punishable by death (Baram), and Amnesty reported dozens of women suspected of prostitution beheaded without trial in October 2000.

majority-settlement.rationale: Expelled Kurdish, Turkman and Assyrian families were replaced with Arab families brought from the south, and Arabs resettling in Kirkuk received land as an incentive (Human Rights Watch 2003).

markets-allocate-better.rationale: The regime ran a centrally planned, state-led economy from 1968, then from 1987 Saddam cut subsidies, sold state firms and said uneconomic state activity must stop, so the record leans against markets but changed late.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Families of soldiers killed in the war with Iran were subsidised for life, given cheap loans and gifts of land as martyrs' benefits (Library of Congress study).

minority-language-support.rationale: Kurdish was official in the autonomous region with its own radio and television, yet the regime banned non-Arab names for newborns in the areas it Arabized (Library of Congress study; Human Rights Watch).

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: A 1974 law set up a Kurdish Autonomous Region with its own assembly and Kurdish as official language, but genuine self-rule never existed there (Library of Congress study).

more-religion-public.rationale: The position changed: after secular rule into the 1980s, the Faith Campaign of 1993-2003 put Qur'an study in schools and the party, built great mosques and enforced public piety (Baram).

national-resource-control.rationale: Saddam presents the 1972 nationalisation of the Iraq Petroleum Company as recovering the country's main wealth from foreign monopolies that had usurped it.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: From 1993 the Qur'an was taught from the first grade, included in the matriculation exam, and teachers were tested on their knowledge of Islam (Baram).

one-party-rule.rationale: The Ba'th dominated the RCC and the Progressive National Front, a single electoral list let it control the National Assembly, and no opposition to its policies was tolerated (Library of Congress study).

open-government-data.rationale: The government rarely published its budgets or plans, releasing only scattered project figures (Library of Congress study).

party-controls-media.rationale: All broadcasting was government controlled, publications were censored to keep them in line with the revolution, and in 2000 the government still kept tight control of all media.

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Saddam says the obstacles facing women are greater than those facing men and blames a degrading view of women inherited from tribal and feudal society.

patriotic-education.rationale: Saddam tells educators to implant belief in the Arab homeland and Palestine and calls for the militarisation of education along the party's principles.

pay-for-effort.rationale: Saddam's 1987 article attacked the labour law for denying people reward according to merit, and he introduced productivity bonuses for state workers (Library of Congress study).

population-transfer.rationale: The regime deported thousands of Shias of Iranian origin to Iran in 1980 and expelled over 94,000 Kurds and Turkmen from Kirkuk and other districts after 1991 (Library of Congress study; Human Rights Watch).

price-controls-essentials.rationale: A 1970 trade regulation made selling goods at prices other than those fixed by the state a felony (Library of Congress study).

profit-exploitation.rationale: The Ninth Congress report states that Iraqis who choose to work for private employers are by no means exploited by them, even when the surplus value goes to the employer.

property-fundamental.rationale: The 1970 agrarian law expropriated holdings above low ceilings with compensation only for improvements, and the state reserved the right to lower the ceiling and dispossess holders (Library of Congress study).

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Property was held as a social function: land above legal ceilings was taken for the people and private business was allowed only where it did not cut across state planning (Library of Congress study).

public-access-to-information.rationale: Economic planning was treated as a state prerogative and the plans as state secrets; budget and planning figures were rarely published (Library of Congress study).

public-ownership.rationale: Under Ba'th rule the state planned the economy and ran heavy industry, banking and oil; the 1987 sell-offs reached bus lines, petrol stations and farms but not the oil sector (Library of Congress study).

rehabilitation.rationale: From 1994 decrees punished theft by amputating the hand and branding the forehead, and the punishments were shown on television for deterrence (Baram; Amnesty).

remove-other-ethnic-groups-from-country.rationale: In 1980 the regime deported thousands of Shias of Iranian origin to Iran (Library of Congress study), while most expelled Kurds were moved inside Iraq.

return-lost-territory.rationale: The 1980 invasion of Iran sought to regain control over the Shatt al-Arab waterway, alongside its wider aims in the Gulf (Library of Congress study).

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: Saddam describes Ba'thism as a call to revive the one Arab nation through unity from the Atlantic to the Gulf, across the existing states.

right-to-secede.rationale: The 1987-89 Anfal campaign against the Kurdish insurgency destroyed some 2,000 villages and killed at least 50,000 non-combatants (Human Rights Watch).

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Amnesty found torture of political detainees systematic and accepted at the highest level, with no attempt to curb it or punish those responsible.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Saddam's 2000 address ranks principles and sacrifice above material things, saying matter does not rank highest in the life of man.

separate-church-state.rationale: The state paid the clergy as officials, built and funded mosques and shrines, and from 1993 put Qur'an teaching in every school (Baram).

separated-powers.rationale: The Revolutionary Command Council held both executive and legislative power, and in practice neither the legislature nor the judiciary was independent of the executive (Library of Congress study).

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Saddam calls Israel the Zionist entity that usurped the land of Palestine and an aggressive entity, not a refuge for persecuted Jews.

state-directs-investment.rationale: The government split its spending into an investment budget serving five-year plans and made fostering heavy industry a constant goal, organising industry into state bodies by subsector (Library of Congress study).

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: The regime never promoted atheism; it paid the clergy and in the 1990s made Qur'an study compulsory in schools (Baram).

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Saddam says he wants Iraq to be a nonaligned country, aligned with no bloc but only against imperialism.

strong-leader.rationale: Power was concentrated in the president and the RCC he chaired, with a pervasive cult of Saddam as the embodiment of the state (Library of Congress study; Malhotra).

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: A 1977 law made men of religion government officials on state salaries, and many clerics were lured or coerced into backing the regime (Baram).

suppress-opposition.rationale: Opposition groups were forced underground by the security police, Ad Dawah membership was made a capital offence in 1980, and suspected opponents were executed into the 2000s.

surveillance-ok.rationale: Satellite dishes and modems were banned, faxes needed permission, and the first internet cafe in 2000 barred unmonitored web email (Human Rights Watch 2001).

term-limits.rationale: The constitution set no term for the president, and Saddam held the office from 1979 until the regime fell in 2003 (Library of Congress study).

territorial-expansion.rationale: Saddam sent his forces into Iran in 1980 to regain the Shatt al-Arab and project Iraqi power over the Gulf and the Arab world (Library of Congress study).

torture-always-illegal.rationale: Amnesty found torture used systematically against political detainees, at a scale that could only result from its acceptance at the highest level.

total-state.rationale: The state planned the economy, controlled all broadcasting and publishing, and the constitution set education the aim of instilling Ba'thist goals (Library of Congress study).

unbreakable-encryption.rationale: When internet access opened in 2000 the authorities banned web email services they could not monitor (Human Rights Watch 2001).

uniformed-youth.rationale: In 2002 families were expelled for refusing to send children aged twelve to seventeen to military training in Saddam's Cubs (Human Rights Watch 2003).

universal-healthcare.rationale: The Library of Congress study records that care in government hospitals and dispensaries and the services of government doctors were free of charge, as the 1970 constitution required.

war-builds-character.rationale: Saddam's 2000 address presents the 1991 war as a trial that raised the Iraqis to new heights of heroism and made their faces 'more luminous'.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Saddam holds that the full emancipation of women cannot be reached without the political, economic and cultural emancipation of the whole society.

women-suffrage.rationale: Women voted in the National Assembly elections, and thirty-three women were elected to the assembly in 1984 (Library of Congress study).

missingStatements.text: A national leader may be honoured in public life through portraits, statues and mass praise as the embodiment of the nation.
missingStatements.rationale: The personality cult of ubiquitous portraits, statues and murals of Saddam is a defining feature of the regime.

missingStatements.text: A state may invade a neighbouring country to recover territory it considers historically part of its own.
missingStatements.rationale: Iraq annexed Kuwait in 1990 as a historic province, and Saddam fought Iran over disputed territory.

notes: Later pass (rules 5) by claude-opus-5-5. The first pass rested on Wikipedia and on sources about Ba'thism in general; this pass rebuilt it from Saddam's own speeches and writings (archive.org copies of the Baghdad translations, 1974-2001), the 1982 Ninth Regional Congress report, the 1970 constitution, and the regime's record as reported by the Library of Congress country study (1988), Human Rights Watch (1992-2004) and Amnesty International (2001), with Baram's study of the regime and religion and Malhotra's article on the term. Record over words: where the regime acted (elections, courts, media, land reform, wars, Arabization, the Faith Campaign) the answer rests on the record alone. Over time: the economy was state-led socialism from 1968 with a partial liberalisation from 1987, and religion turned from secular rule to the 1993-2003 Faith Campaign, an explicit change sustained for a decade, which the religion answers follow. Every first-pass answer was rechecked; those the new sources do not settle are nulled. Blocked: the Washington Institute (s5), the US State Department human rights reports, refworld, FPRI and DTIC refused scripted access, and Bengio's Saddam's Word, Sassoon's Saddam Hussein's Ba'th Party and Saddam's On Social and Foreign Affairs in Iraq were available only as lending copies. Themes searched: economy (planning, property, land reform, wages, unions, prices, oil, foreign capital), government (party, elections, RCC, courts, presidency, autonomy), society (women, education, religion, minorities, Arabization), liberty (media, internet, death penalty, torture, punishments), world (wars, the UN, Palestine, non-alignment, Arab unity, nuclear programme). Ecology, technology and most questions of social policy stay null: the sources say nothing on them.
